 By Stephanie Reid Published on November 07, 2026 Orlando Central Business District — Weather Coverage Backdrop
Google Street View Orlando’s forecast for Saturday, Nov. 7, calls for mostly sunny skies and a high near 82 degrees after temperatures near 72 early in the day. But the pleasant inland weather coincides with serious water hazards elsewhere in Central Florida: a high risk of life-threatening rip currents along Atlantic beaches and continued flooding along the St. Johns River.
 Warm, mostly dry weather through midweek
 The National Weather Service in Melbourne forecasts north winds of 5 to 10 mph Saturday, with a brief shower or patchy fog possible around daybreak before drier air settles in. Saturday night should be mostly clear, with a low near 61. Sunday is expected to be mostly sunny with a high near 81; Monday and Tuesday should be sunny or mostly sunny, with highs around 80 and overnight lows near 60 to 63. Wednesday is forecast to be partly sunny and warm, while showers become possible Thursday and Friday, when highs are expected near 75 and 71, respectively.
 Beach and river hazards persist
 The National Weather Service in Melbourne warns of a high risk of life-threatening rip currents along Central Florida’s Atlantic beaches and advises people to stay out of the ocean. A long-period swell and higher morning tides could also cause minor to moderate coastal flooding near and south of St. Lucie Inlet, according to the agency .
 Flood warnings remain in effect at St. Johns River forecast points near Sanford, DeLand, Astor and Cocoa. The river is expected to keep rising; Cocoa is forecast to reach major flood stage this weekend, while Geneva could approach major flood stage next week, the National Weather Service says .
 Historical records offer context, not a direct comparison
 High water on the St. Johns has caused prolonged flooding before. In a separate 2022 episode, the river at Astor crested on Oct. 1, breaking an 89-year-old record. WUSF reported that Hurricane Ian’s heavy rains worsened the flooding and that Hurricane Nicole later made conditions worse. Astor is among the current forecast points, but the current forecast information does not give a crest measurement that can be directly compared with the 2022 record.
 A separate historical benchmark comes from further south: the National Weather Service Melbourne reported that Tropical Storm Fay, in August 2008, brought the St. Johns River near Cocoa to a peak of 17.09 feet, then the third-highest crest on record. That past measurement provides local flood history, not a prediction of how high the river will reach this weekend.
 Rip currents are a recurring hazard even when skies are clear. NOAA Ocean Today explains that strong currents can occur on sunny days and advises beachgoers to check local conditions, wave forecasts and tides before entering the water. Separately, USA Today reported that 66 people died in rip currents across the United States and its territories in the year covered by its report, including at least 19 on Florida beaches. Those figures are broader historical context, not deaths reported for this weekend. For the current local warning, the National Weather Service’s advice is to stay out of the ocean.
 For Orlando-area residents, the forecast offers several mostly dry days for outdoor plans, but sunny weather inland does not remove the risks at the coast or along the river. Avoid flooded areas, follow local officials’ guidance and never drive through standing floodwater.
